The maritime fur trade (historically called the North West trade), a ship-based fur trade system, focused largely on acquiring furs of sea otters and other animals from the Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast and Alaska Natives. Entrepreneurs also exploited fur-bearing skins from the wider Pacific and the Southern Ocean.
The trade mostly serviced the market in Qing China, which imported furs and exported tea, silks, porcelain, and other Chinese goods to Europe and the United States.

The trade was pioneered by the Russians. Through the Siberian fur trade, they reached the Pacific in the 17th century, then moved eastward, reaching the Alaska Peninsula by the 1760s. The Spanish began trading in 1774, the British in 1778, and the Americans in 1788. Russians controlled the Alaskan coast during this era.

The coast further south saw fierce competition between British and American traders. The British were the first to operate in the southern sector, but the Americans dominated from the 1790s to the 1830s. Once the British Hudson's Bay Company (HBC) entered the trade in the 1820s, they outcompeted the Americans by about 1840.
